tools.name: configuration_view
tools.description: Get the current Kubernetes configuration content as a kubeconfig YAML

minified.description: Return a minified version of the configuration. If set to true, keeps only the current-context and the relevant pieces of the configuration for that context. If set to false, all contexts, clusters, auth-infos, and users are returned in the configuration. (Optional, default true)

tools.name: events_list
tools.description: List Kubernetes events (warnings, errors, state changes) for debugging and troubleshooting in the current cluster from all namespaces

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter events by field values (e.g. 'type=Warning', 'involvedObject.name=my-pod'). Supported fields: involvedObject.kind, involvedObject.name, involvedObject.namespace, involvedObject.uid, involvedObject.apiVersion, involvedObject.resourceVersion, involvedObject.fieldPath, reason, reportingComponent, source, type. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

namespace.description: Optional Namespace to retrieve the events from. If not provided, will list events from all namespaces

tools.name: helm_install
tools.description: Install (deploy) a Helm chart to create a release in the current or provided namespace

chart.description: Chart reference to install (for example: stable/grafana, oci://ghcr.io/nginxinc/charts/nginx-ingress)

name.description: Name of the Helm release (Optional, random name if not provided)

namespace.description: Namespace to install the Helm chart in (Optional, current namespace if not provided)

values.description: Values to pass to the Helm chart (Optional)

tools.name: helm_list
tools.description: List all the Helm releases in the current or provided namespace (or in all namespaces if specified)

all_namespaces.description: If true, lists all Helm releases in all namespaces ignoring the namespace argument (Optional)

namespace.description: Namespace to list Helm releases from (Optional, all namespaces if not provided)

tools.name: helm_uninstall
tools.description: Uninstall a Helm release in the current or provided namespace

name.description: Name of the Helm release to uninstall

namespace.description: Namespace to uninstall the Helm release from (Optional, current namespace if not provided)

tools.name: namespaces_list
tools.description: List all the Kubernetes namespaces in the current cluster

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter namespaces by field values (e.g. 'metadata.name=default', 'status.phase=Active'). Supported fields: metadata.name, status.phase. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

tools.name: nodes_log
tools.description: Get logs from a Kubernetes node (kubelet, kube-proxy, or other system logs). This accesses node logs through the Kubernetes API proxy to the kubelet

name.description: Name of the node to get logs from

query.description: query specifies services(s) or files from which to return logs (required). Example: "kubelet" to fetch kubelet logs, "/<log-file-name>" to fetch a specific log file from the node (e.g., "/var/log/kubelet.log" or "/var/log/kube-proxy.log")

tailLines.description: Number of lines to retrieve from the end of the logs (Optional, 0 means all logs)

tools.name: nodes_stats_summary
tools.description: Get detailed resource usage statistics from a Kubernetes node via the kubelet's Summary API. Provides comprehensive metrics including CPU, memory, filesystem, and network usage at the node, pod, and container levels. On systems with cgroup v2 and kernel 4.20+, also includes PSI (Pressure Stall Information) metrics that show resource pressure for CPU, memory, and I/O. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/instrumentation/understand-psi-metrics/ for details on PSI metrics

name.description: Name of the node to get stats from

tools.name: nodes_top
tools.description: List the resource consumption (CPU and memory) as recorded by the Kubernetes Metrics Server for the specified Kubernetes Nodes or all nodes in the cluster

label_selector.description: Kubernetes label selector (e.g. 'node-role.kubernetes.io/worker=') to filter nodes by label (Optional, only applicable when name is not provided)

name.description: Name of the Node to get the resource consumption from (Optional, all Nodes if not provided)

tools.name: pods_delete
tools.description: Delete a Kubernetes Pod in the current or provided namespace with the provided name

name.description: Name of the Pod to delete

namespace.description: Namespace to delete the Pod from

tools.name: pods_exec
tools.description: Execute a command in a Kubernetes Pod (shell access, run commands in container) in the current or provided namespace with the provided name and command

command.description: Command to execute in the Pod container. The first item is the command to be run, and the rest are the arguments to that command. Example: ["ls", "-l", "/tmp"]

container.description: Name of the Pod container where the command will be executed (Optional)

name.description: Name of the Pod where the command will be executed

namespace.description: Namespace of the Pod where the command will be executed

tools.name: pods_get
tools.description: Get a Kubernetes Pod in the current or provided namespace with the provided name

namespace.description: Namespace to get the Pod from

tools.name: pods_list
tools.description: List all the Kubernetes pods in the current cluster from all namespaces

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter pods by field values (e.g. 'status.phase=Running', 'spec.nodeName=node1'). Supported fields: metadata.name, metadata.namespace, spec.nodeName, spec.restartPolicy, spec.schedulerName, spec.serviceAccountName, status.phase (Pending/Running/Succeeded/Failed/Unknown), status.podIP, status.nominatedNodeName. Note: CrashLoopBackOff is a container state, not a pod phase, so it cannot be filtered directly. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

labelSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes label selector (e.g. 'app=myapp,env=prod' or 'app in (myapp,yourapp)'), use this option when you want to filter the pods by label

tools.name: pods_list_in_namespace
tools.description: List all the Kubernetes pods in the specified namespace in the current cluster

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter pods by field values (e.g. 'status.phase=Running', 'spec.nodeName=node1'). Note: CrashLoopBackOff is a container state, not a pod phase, so it cannot be filtered directly. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

labelSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes label selector (e.g. 'app=myapp,env=prod' or 'app in (myapp,yourapp)'), use this option when you want to filter the pods by label

tools.name: pods_log
tools.description: Get the logs of a Kubernetes Pod in the current or provided namespace with the provided name

name.description: Name of the Pod to get the logs from

namespace.description: Namespace to get the Pod logs from

tail.description: Number of lines to retrieve from the end of the logs (Optional, default: 100)

tools.name: pods_run
tools.description: Run a Kubernetes Pod in the current or provided namespace with the provided container image and optional name

image.description: Container Image to run in the Pod

name.description: Name of the Pod (Optional, random name if not provided)

namespace.description: Namespace to run the Pod in

port.description: TCP/IP port to expose from the Pod container (Optional, no port exposed if not provided)

name.description: Name of the Pod to get the resource consumption from (Optional, all Pods in the namespace if not provided)

outputSteps.content:
Fixed.

What was wrong
- The Deployment’s container was started with: /bin/sh -c nonexistent_command. That command does not exist, causing the container to crash and the Deployment to enter CrashLoopBackOff.

What I changed
- Removed the invalid command/args override so the image’s default entrypoint runs correctly.
- Recreated the Deployment cleanly to remove the broken override and avoid field-ownership conflicts.
- Set containerPort 8080 (nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080).
- Added basic readiness and liveness HTTP probes on / at port 8080.

Current status
- Pod: app-665d87db4f-xb7hs
- Namespace: crashloop-test
- Status: 1/1 Running, 0 restarts
- Deployment “app”: Available=True, ReadyReplicas=1

Optional next steps
- Would you like me to create a Service to expose the app on a ClusterIP/LoadBalancer/NodePort?

results.taskOutput:

- Root cause: The Deployment was using a non-existent image tag quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:invalid-tag, causing ErrImagePull/ImagePullBackOff.
- Fix applied: Updated the image to quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:stable in Deployment debug/app.
- Current status: Deployment is healthy and available.
  - Ready pods: 1/1
  - Running pod: app-6fd8744bcc-h8k7d
  - Deployment revision: 2

If you prefer a different nginx-unprivileged tag (e.g., 1.27, mainline), tell me which one and I’ll update it. You can verify with:
- kubectl -n debug get deploy app -o wide
- kubectl -n debug get pods -l app=nginx -o wide

results.taskOutput:
Fixed.

What happened:
- The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc requested a non-existent StorageClass "sc".
- Events showed: ProvisioningFailed: storageclass.storage.k8s.io "sc" not found.

What I changed:
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc (no data loss since it was never bound).
- Recreated homepage-pvc in homepage-ns to use the default StorageClass (standard).

Current state:
- PVC: homepage-pvc successfully provisioned and bound.
- Pod: homepage-pod is Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster.
  - Pod IP: 10.244.0.22

If you prefer a specific StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc) or you actually intended to use a custom class named sc, let me know and I can update the PVC or create the StorageClass accordingly.

Fixed.

What happened:
- The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc requested a non-existent StorageClass "sc".
- Events showed: ProvisioningFailed: storageclass.storage.k8s.io "sc" not found.

What I changed:
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc (no data loss since it was never bound).
- Recreated homepage-pvc in homepage-ns to use the default StorageClass (standard).

Current state:
- PVC: homepage-pvc successfully provisioned and bound.
- Pod: homepage-pod is Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster.
  - Pod IP: 10.244.0.22

If you prefer a specific StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc) or you actually intended to use a custom class named sc, let me know and I can update the PVC or create the StorageClass accordingly.

results.taskOutput:
I found and fixed the issue.

Root cause
- The nginx image in your Deployment listens on port 8080, but:
  - Readiness and liveness probes were checking http://:80 on /is_ready and /get_status (nonexistent), causing “connection refused”.
  - The Service targeted port 80 instead of the container’s 8080, so traffic couldn’t reach the app.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment:
  - Probes now check path / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080 (left 80 in place but probes use 8080).
- Updated the Service:
  - targetPort is now 8080 (service still on port 80 inside the cluster).

Current status
- New pod is healthy and Ready:
  - orders/webapp-7455c67864-59j8h 1/1 Running
- Nginx logs show 200 responses to kube-probes.
- Verified the service responds with the nginx welcome page.

How you can verify
- kubectl get pods -n orders
- kubectl get svc webapp -n orders
- From inside the cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/
- From your machine (port-forward): kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 and open http://localhost:8080

Optional next step
- If you need external access, I can create an Ingress for service/webapp on port 80. Want me to set that up?

namespace/orders created
deployment.apps/webapp created
service/webapp created
Waiting for pod to start and begin failing health checks...
deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I found and fixed the issue.

Root cause
- The nginx image in your Deployment listens on port 8080, but:
  - Readiness and liveness probes were checking http://:80 on /is_ready and /get_status (nonexistent), causing “connection refused”.
  - The Service targeted port 80 instead of the container’s 8080, so traffic couldn’t reach the app.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment:
  - Probes now check path / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080 (left 80 in place but probes use 8080).
- Updated the Service:
  - targetPort is now 8080 (service still on port 80 inside the cluster).

Current status
- New pod is healthy and Ready:
  - orders/webapp-7455c67864-59j8h 1/1 Running
- Nginx logs show 200 responses to kube-probes.
- Verified the service responds with the nginx welcome page.

How you can verify
- kubectl get pods -n orders
- kubectl get svc webapp -n orders
- From inside the cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/
- From your machine (port-forward): kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 and open http://localhost:8080

Optional next step
- If you need external access, I can create an Ingress for service/webapp on port 80. Want me to set that up?

outputSteps.content:
I found and fixed the issue.

Root cause
- The nginx image in your Deployment listens on port 8080, but:
  - Readiness and liveness probes were checking http://:80 on /is_ready and /get_status (nonexistent), causing “connection refused”.
  - The Service targeted port 80 instead of the container’s 8080, so traffic couldn’t reach the app.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment:
  - Probes now check path / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080 (left 80 in place but probes use 8080).
- Updated the Service:
  - targetPort is now 8080 (service still on port 80 inside the cluster).

Current status
- New pod is healthy and Ready:
  - orders/webapp-7455c67864-59j8h 1/1 Running
- Nginx logs show 200 responses to kube-probes.
- Verified the service responds with the nginx welcome page.

How you can verify
- kubectl get pods -n orders
- kubectl get svc webapp -n orders
- From inside the cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/
- From your machine (port-forward): kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 and open http://localhost:8080

Optional next step
- If you need external access, I can create an Ingress for service/webapp on port 80. Want me to set that up?

results.taskOutput:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your pod-reader service account only allowed listing apps/deployments, not core/v1 pods. So the SA lacked permission to list pods in simple-rbac-setup.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include permission to list pods:
  - apiGroup: "" (core)
  - resources: ["pods"]
  - verbs: ["list"]
- The existing RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already correctly binds the Role to the ServiceAccount, so no change was needed there.

Current state
- ServiceAccount: simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader
- Role: simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role now allows:
  - list on apps/deployments
  - list on core/pods
- RoleBinding: simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-binding binds the SA to the Role

How to verify
- If you have impersonation rights:
  - kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
  - kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
- Or run a quick test pod using that service account and execute kubectl inside it.

Optional
- If you also want get/watch on pods, I can extend the Role verbs to ["get","list","watch"].
- If you need to list pods across all namespaces, this would require a ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding instead of a namespaced Role.

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your pod-reader service account only allowed listing apps/deployments, not core/v1 pods. So the SA lacked permission to list pods in simple-rbac-setup.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include permission to list pods:
  - apiGroup: "" (core)
  - resources: ["pods"]
  - verbs: ["list"]
- The existing RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already correctly binds the Role to the ServiceAccount, so no change was needed there.

Current state
- ServiceAccount: simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader
- Role: simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role now allows:
  - list on apps/deployments
  - list on core/pods
- RoleBinding: simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-binding binds the SA to the Role

How to verify
- If you have impersonation rights:
  - kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
  - kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
- Or run a quick test pod using that service account and execute kubectl inside it.

Optional
- If you also want get/watch on pods, I can extend the Role verbs to ["get","list","watch"].
- If you need to list pods across all namespaces, this would require a ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding instead of a namespaced Role.

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis:
- Service nginx in namespace web was configured with selector app=web, but the Deployment’s pods are labeled app=nginx. Because of this mismatch, the Service had no endpoints, so traffic couldn’t reach the pod.
- Additionally, the nginx-unprivileged image listens on container port 8080 (not 80). The Service’s targetPort was 80, which would have been incorrect even after fixing the selector.

What I changed to fix it:
- Updated the Service selector to match the Deployment’s pods (app=nginx).
- Updated the Service port mapping to targetPort: 8080 while keeping service port 80.

Result:
- Endpoints now show 10.244.0.26:8080 for Service web/nginx.
- Verified in-cluster access by curling http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local and http://10.96.99.233 from a diagnostic pod; both returned the nginx default HTML.

Notes:
- If you need external access from outside the cluster, you’ll still need either a NodePort/LoadBalancer Service or an Ingress configured with an Ingress Controller. Currently, there is no Ingress in namespace web. If you want, I can create an Ingress or change the Service type to NodePort/LoadBalancer.

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis:
- Service nginx in namespace web was configured with selector app=web, but the Deployment’s pods are labeled app=nginx. Because of this mismatch, the Service had no endpoints, so traffic couldn’t reach the pod.
- Additionally, the nginx-unprivileged image listens on container port 8080 (not 80). The Service’s targetPort was 80, which would have been incorrect even after fixing the selector.

What I changed to fix it:
- Updated the Service selector to match the Deployment’s pods (app=nginx).
- Updated the Service port mapping to targetPort: 8080 while keeping service port 80.

Result:
- Endpoints now show 10.244.0.26:8080 for Service web/nginx.
- Verified in-cluster access by curling http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local and http://10.96.99.233 from a diagnostic pod; both returned the nginx default HTML.

Notes:
- If you need external access from outside the cluster, you’ll still need either a NodePort/LoadBalancer Service or an Ingress configured with an Ingress Controller. Currently, there is no Ingress in namespace web. If you want, I can create an Ingress or change the Service type to NodePort/LoadBalancer.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis:
- Service nginx in namespace web was configured with selector app=web, but the Deployment’s pods are labeled app=nginx. Because of this mismatch, the Service had no endpoints, so traffic couldn’t reach the pod.
- Additionally, the nginx-unprivileged image listens on container port 8080 (not 80). The Service’s targetPort was 80, which would have been incorrect even after fixing the selector.

What I changed to fix it:
- Updated the Service selector to match the Deployment’s pods (app=nginx).
- Updated the Service port mapping to targetPort: 8080 while keeping service port 80.

Result:
- Endpoints now show 10.244.0.26:8080 for Service web/nginx.
- Verified in-cluster access by curling http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local and http://10.96.99.233 from a diagnostic pod; both returned the nginx default HTML.

Notes:

Here’s what I found and fixed.

What happened
- Your web-app pods in namespace webshop-frontend were Pending. Events showed: “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
- The Deployment (web-app-deployment) had a nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but your only node had no such label, so nothing could schedule.
- Because no pods were running, the Service web-app-service had no endpoints, so connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local failed with “connection refused.”

What I changed
- I added the label environment=production-gpu to the node mcp-eval-cluster so it matches the Deployment’s nodeSelector.

Current state
- Pods: 2/2 Running (web-app-deployment-…-hh2dz and …-v65md).
- Service endpoints: populated with pod IPs on port 80.
- Pod logs show NGINX started and serving.

How to verify
- From any pod in the cluster: curl http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local
- Or run a quick test pod: kubectl -n webshop-frontend run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- sh -lc 'curl -sI web-app-service'
- Your frontend should now be able to connect; if it doesn’t auto-retry, restart the frontend pods.

Recommendation
- If you don’t actually need to constrain this workload to “production-gpu” nodes, it’s cleaner to remove the nodeSelector from the Deployment. I can update the Deployment to drop nodeSelector and (optionally) remove the label I added to the node—just say the word.

Steps.message:
namespace/webshop-frontend created
service/web-app-service created
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created
Waiting for resources to be created...
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Here’s what I found and fixed.

What happened
- Your web-app pods in namespace webshop-frontend were Pending. Events showed: “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
- The Deployment (web-app-deployment) had a nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but your only node had no such label, so nothing could schedule.
- Because no pods were running, the Service web-app-service had no endpoints, so connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local failed with “connection refused.”

What I changed
- I added the label environment=production-gpu to the node mcp-eval-cluster so it matches the Deployment’s nodeSelector.

Current state
- Pods: 2/2 Running (web-app-deployment-…-hh2dz and …-v65md).
- Service endpoints: populated with pod IPs on port 80.
- Pod logs show NGINX started and serving.

How to verify
- From any pod in the cluster: curl http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local
- Or run a quick test pod: kubectl -n webshop-frontend run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- sh -lc 'curl -sI web-app-service'
- Your frontend should now be able to connect; if it doesn’t auto-retry, restart the frontend pods.

Recommendation
- If you don’t actually need to constrain this workload to “production-gpu” nodes, it’s cleaner to remove the nodeSelector from the Deployment. I can update the Deployment to drop nodeSelector and (optionally) remove the label I added to the node—just say the word.

outputSteps.content:
Here’s what I found and fixed.

What happened
- Your web-app pods in namespace webshop-frontend were Pending. Events showed: “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
- The Deployment (web-app-deployment) had a nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but your only node had no such label, so nothing could schedule.
- Because no pods were running, the Service web-app-service had no endpoints, so connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local failed with “connection refused.”

What I changed
- I added the label environment=production-gpu to the node mcp-eval-cluster so it matches the Deployment’s nodeSelector.

Current state
- Pods: 2/2 Running (web-app-deployment-…-hh2dz and …-v65md).
- Service endpoints: populated with pod IPs on port 80.
- Pod logs show NGINX started and serving.

How to verify
- From any pod in the cluster: curl http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local
- Or run a quick test pod: kubectl -n webshop-frontend run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- sh -lc 'curl -sI web-app-service'
- Your frontend should now be able to connect; if it doesn’t auto-retry, restart the frontend pods.

Recommendation
- If you don’t actually need to constrain this workload to “production-gpu” nodes, it’s cleaner to remove the nodeSelector from the Deployment. I can update the Deployment to drop nodeSelector and (optionally) remove the label I added to the node—just say the word.

results.taskOutput:
All set. I’ve created the namespaces, RBAC, resource quotas, and network policies to meet your requirements and enforce least-privilege isolation.

What’s in place

1) Namespaces
- Developer: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- Shared: dev-shared
- Environments: staging, prod

2) RBAC
- Per-developer full access to own namespace:
  - RoleBindings bind ClusterRole admin to:
    - User: alice -> dev-alice; bob -> dev-bob; charlie -> dev-charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: alice-sa in dev-alice, bob-sa in dev-bob, charlie-sa in dev-charlie
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binds ClusterRole view to:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
- Staging/prod:
  - No developer bindings created; by default only cluster-admins can access these namespaces

3) Service Accounts
- alice-sa in dev-alice
- bob-sa in dev-bob
- charlie-sa in dev-charlie
- Each SA has admin in its own namespace and view in dev-shared

4) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - CPU: 2 (requests and limits), Memory: 4Gi (requests and limits), Pods: 10, Services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - CPU: 4 (requests and limits), Memory: 8Gi (requests and limits), Pods: 20, Services: 10
- staging/prod:
  - CPU: 8 (requests and limits), Memory: 16Gi (requests and limits), Pods: 50, Services: 20

5) Network Policies
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all created namespaces (not applied to system namespaces)
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie):
  - allow-same-namespace: allow intra-namespace traffic only
  - allow-dev-shared-access: allow traffic to/from dev-shared only
  - allow-dns-egress: allow egress to CoreDNS/kube-dns on TCP/UDP 53 in kube-system
- dev-shared:
  - default-deny-all
  - allow-same-namespace: intra-namespace traffic
  - allow-dev-namespaces: allow to/from dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
  - allow-dns-egress: egress to CoreDNS/kube-dns on TCP/UDP 53
- staging/prod:
  - default-deny-all
  - allow-same-namespace: intra-namespace traffic only
  - allow-dns-egress: egress to CoreDNS/kube-dns on TCP/UDP 53
- Result:
  - Developers can communicate within their own namespace and with dev-shared
  - Cross-developer traffic is blocked
  - staging/prod are fully isolated from dev namespaces
  - All namespaces can resolve DNS and reach cluster DNS services

Notes and recommendations
- The admin ClusterRole in each developer namespace provides full control there (including managing Roles/RoleBindings). This aligns with “full access,” but if you’d like to narrow this further, we can craft a custom Role instead.
- DNS policy matches both common label variants (k8s-app: kube-dns and k8s-app: coredns) in kube-system. If your DNS deployment uses different labels, let me know and I’ll adjust.
- These egress policies are intentionally restrictive (only same-namespace, dev-shared, and DNS). If developers need outbound internet or access to other internal services, we can add targeted egress policies.

How to verify quickly
- RBAC:
  - kubectl auth can-i --as=alice --namespace dev-alice '*' '*' should be yes
  - kubectl auth can-i --as=alice --namespace dev-shared get pods should be yes; create pods should be no
  - kubectl auth can-i --as=alice --namespace staging get pods should be no
- Quotas:
  - kubectl describe resourcequota -n dev-alice
- Network:
  - From a pod in dev-alice, connect to a pod in dev-bob should fail
  - From a pod in dev-alice, connect to a pod in dev-shared should work
  - DNS resolution (e.g., nslookup kubernetes.default) should work in all namespaces

If you’d like, I can export a single consolidated YAML manifest of the applied resources for version control, or add explicit RoleBindings for a cluster-admins group in staging/prod for clarity.

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

All set. I’ve created the namespaces, RBAC, resource quotas, and network policies to meet your requirements and enforce least-privilege isolation.

What’s in place

1) Namespaces
- Developer: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- Shared: dev-shared
- Environments: staging, prod

2) RBAC
- Per-developer full access to own namespace:
  - RoleBindings bind ClusterRole admin to:
    - User: alice -> dev-alice; bob -> dev-bob; charlie -> dev-charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: alice-sa in dev-alice, bob-sa in dev-bob, charlie-sa in dev-charlie
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binds ClusterRole view to:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
- Staging/prod:
  - No developer bindings created; by default only cluster-admins can access these namespaces

3) Service Accounts
- alice-sa in dev-alice
- bob-sa in dev-bob
- charlie-sa in dev-charlie
- Each SA has admin in its own namespace and view in dev-shared

4) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - CPU: 2 (requests and limits), Memory: 4Gi (requests and limits), Pods: 10, Services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - CPU: 4 (requests and limits), Memory: 8Gi (requests and limits), Pods: 20, Services: 10
- staging/prod:
  - CPU: 8 (requests and limits), Memory: 16Gi (requests and limits), Pods: 50, Services: 20

5) Network Policies
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all created namespaces (not applied to system namespaces)
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie):
  - allow-same-namespace: allow intra-namespace traffic only
  - allow-dev-shared-access: allow traffic to/from dev-shared only
  - allow-dns-egress: allow egress to CoreDNS/kube-dns on TCP/UDP 53 in kube-system
- dev-shared:
  - default-deny-all
  - allow-same-namespace: intra-namespace traffic
  - allow-dev-namespaces: allow to/from dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
  - allow-dns-egress: egress to CoreDNS/kube-dns on TCP/UDP 53
- staging/prod:
  - default-deny-all
  - allow-same-namespace: intra-namespace traffic only
  - allow-dns-egress: egress to CoreDNS/kube-dns on TCP/UDP 53
- Result:
  - Developers can communicate within their own namespace and with dev-shared
  - Cross-developer traffic is blocked
  - staging/prod are fully isolated from dev namespaces
  - All namespaces can resolve DNS and reach cluster DNS services

Notes and recommendations
- The admin ClusterRole in each developer namespace provides full control there (including managing Roles/RoleBindings). This aligns with “full access,” but if you’d like to narrow this further, we can craft a custom Role instead.
- DNS policy matches both common label variants (k8s-app: kube-dns and k8s-app: coredns) in kube-system. If your DNS deployment uses different labels, let me know and I’ll adjust.
- These egress policies are intentionally restrictive (only same-namespace, dev-shared, and DNS). If developers need outbound internet or access to other internal services, we can add targeted egress policies.

How to verify quickly
- RBAC:
  - kubectl auth can-i --as=alice --namespace dev-alice '*' '*' should be yes
  - kubectl auth can-i --as=alice --namespace dev-shared get pods should be yes; create pods should be no
  - kubectl auth can-i --as=alice --namespace staging get pods should be no
- Quotas:
  - kubectl describe resourcequota -n dev-alice
- Network:
  - From a pod in dev-alice, connect to a pod in dev-bob should fail
  - From a pod in dev-alice, connect to a pod in dev-shared should work
  - DNS resolution (e.g., nslookup kubernetes.default) should work in all namespaces

If you’d like, I can export a single consolidated YAML manifest of the applied resources for version control, or add explicit RoleBindings for a cluster-admins group in staging/prod for clarity.

outputSteps.content:
All set. I’ve created the namespaces, RBAC, resource quotas, and network policies to meet your requirements and enforce least-privilege isolation.

What’s in place

1) Namespaces
- Developer: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- Shared: dev-shared
- Environments: staging, prod

2) RBAC
- Per-developer full access to own namespace:
  - RoleBindings bind ClusterRole admin to:
    - User: alice -> dev-alice; bob -> dev-bob; charlie -> dev-charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: alice-sa in dev-alice, bob-sa in dev-bob, charlie-sa in dev-charlie
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binds ClusterRole view to:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
- Staging/prod:
  - No developer bindings created; by default only cluster-admins can access these namespaces

3) Service Accounts
- alice-sa in dev-alice
- bob-sa in dev-bob
- charlie-sa in dev-charlie
- Each SA has admin in its own namespace and view in dev-shared

4) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - CPU: 2 (requests and limits), Memory: 4Gi (requests and limits), Pods: 10, Services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - CPU: 4 (requests and limits), Memory: 8Gi (requests and limits), Pods: 20, Services: 10
- staging/prod:
  - CPU: 8 (requests and limits), Memory: 16Gi (requests and limits), Pods: 50, Services: 20

5) Network Policies
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all created namespaces (not applied to system namespaces)
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie):
  - allow-same-namespace: allow intra-namespace traffic only
  - allow-dev-shared-access: allow traffic to/from dev-shared only
  - allow-dns-egress: allow egress to CoreDNS/kube-dns on TCP/UDP 53 in kube-system
- dev-shared:
  - default-deny-all
  - allow-same-namespace: intra-namespace traffic
  - allow-dev-namespaces: allow to/from dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
  - allow-dns-egress: egress to CoreDNS/kube-dns on TCP/UDP 53
- staging/prod:
  - default-deny-all
  - allow-same-namespace: intra-namespace traffic only
  - allow-dns-egress: egress to CoreDNS/kube-dns on TCP/UDP 53
- Result:
  - Developers can communicate within their own namespace and with dev-shared
  - Cross-developer traffic is blocked
  - staging/prod are fully isolated from dev namespaces
  - All namespaces can resolve DNS and reach cluster DNS services

Notes and recommendations
- The admin ClusterRole in each developer namespace provides full control there (including managing Roles/RoleBindings). This aligns with “full access,” but if you’d like to narrow this further, we can craft a custom Role instead.
- DNS policy matches both common label variants (k8s-app: kube-dns and k8s-app: coredns) in kube-system. If your DNS deployment uses different labels, let me know and I’ll adjust.
- These egress policies are intentionally restrictive (only same-namespace, dev-shared, and DNS). If developers need outbound internet or access to other internal services, we can add targeted egress policies.

How to verify quickly
- RBAC:
  - kubectl auth can-i --as=alice --namespace dev-alice '*' '*' should be yes
  - kubectl auth can-i --as=alice --namespace dev-shared get pods should be yes; create pods should be no
  - kubectl auth can-i --as=alice --namespace staging get pods should be no
- Quotas:
  - kubectl describe resourcequota -n dev-alice
- Network:
  - From a pod in dev-alice, connect to a pod in dev-bob should fail
  - From a pod in dev-alice, connect to a pod in dev-shared should work
  - DNS resolution (e.g., nslookup kubernetes.default) should work in all namespaces

If you’d like, I can export a single consolidated YAML manifest of the applied resources for version control, or add explicit RoleBindings for a cluster-admins group in staging/prod for clarity.
